Mustafa II: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1695 to 1703. Mustafa II (Ottoman Turkish: مصطفى ثانى Muṣṭafā-yi sānī; 6 February 1664 – 29 December 1703) was the sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1695 to 1703.
Born into a prominent Catholic mandarin family, he became South Vietnam's first president in 1955 and ruled until his assassination during a CIA-backed coup in 1963 — who was he?

Ngo Dinh Diem: President of South Vietnam from 1955 to 1963. Diệm was born into a prominent Catholic family with his father, Ngô Đình Khả, being a high-ranking mandarin for Emperor Thành Thái during the French colonial era.

Born a Danish prince at Sandringham House in England, this future Norwegian king became heir apparent when his father was elected to the throne in 1905, and led as defence chief during WWII — who is he?
Olav V: King of Norway from 1957 to 1991.
Born Mukunda Lal Ghosh, this Indian-American monk founded the Self-Realization Fellowship and is considered the 'Father of Yoga in the West' — who is he?
Paramahansa Yogananda: Indian and American yogi and guru (1893–1952)

The younger brother of Louis XIV and founder of a cadet branch of the House of Bourbon, this 17th-century French royal, known simply as 'Monsieur,' won a notable military victory over William of Orange at the Battle of Cassel. Who was he?
Philippe I, Duke of Orléans: French prince (1640–1701)
A member of India's storied Nehru dynasty, this Indian National Congress politician has represented Wayanad in Kerala in the Lok Sabha since November 2024 — who is she?

As Sweden's special envoy in Budapest in 1944 he saved thousands of Jews with protective passports and "Swedish territory" safe houses, then vanished in 1945 after Soviet SMERSH agents detained him — who was this humanitarian diplomat?
Raoul Wallenberg: Swedish diplomat and humanitarian (1912–1945). Raoul Wallenberg (4 August 1912 – disappeared 17 January 1945) was a Swedish architect, businessman, diplomat, and humanitarian.
The longest-serving prime minister in Slovak history, he has led the country across four separate terms since founding his left-wing party in 1999 — who is he?
Prince Albert Victor, Duke of Clarence and Avondale
Robert Fico: Prime Minister of Slovakia (2006–2010, 2012–2018, 2023–present)
After serving as Prime Minister of Kuwait from 1978 to 2006, this royal briefly became Emir for just nine days before abdicating — who is he?
Saad Al-Salim Al-Sabah: Emir of Kuwait in 2006.
Governor of five different Indian states over his career, this politician was serving as the final governor of Jammu and Kashmir when its special status was revoked in 2019 — who is he?
In Hinduism, what name is given to the feminine 'Universal Power' that complements Shiva and is worshipped at shrines called pithas?
Shakti: Divine feminine energy in Hinduism.
Born in 1955, this Princess Royal of Thailand is the second daughter of King Bhumibol Adulyadej and the younger sister of King Vajiralongkorn — who is she?
Sirindhorn: Thai princess (born 1955). Maha Chakri Sirindhorn, The Princess Royal (born 2 April 1955) is a member of the Thai royal family.
In 1956, Britain, France, and Israel jointly invaded Egypt after Nasser nationalized a vital canal — what is this conflict commonly called?
Suez Crisis: 1956 British–French–Israeli invasion of Egypt.
The son of Odysseus and Penelope, this young man sailed to Pylos and Sparta seeking news of his father, then helped slay the suitors back home in Ithaca — who is he?
Telemachus: Mythological son of Odysseus. When Telemachus reached manhood, he visited Pylos and Sparta in search of his wandering father.

Beginning with the death of Russia's last Rurik ruler in 1598 and ending with the Romanov dynasty's rise in 1613, this era of famine, false pretenders, and foreign occupation devastated Russia — what is it called?
Time of Troubles: 1598–1613 chaotic period of Russian history.
In 2023, 1.3 million applicants competed for just 1,255 government job openings through this Indian constitutional body's exams — what is it?
Union Public Service Commission: India's central recruiting agency.

Ruling for just eight months during the chaotic Year of the Four Emperors, this Roman ruler took the honorific Germanicus instead of Caesar and tried to boost his popularity by imitating the still-beloved Nero — who was he?
Carved out of the Carolingian Empire at the Treaty of Verdun in 843 and lasting until the Capetians took over in 987, which kingdom was the very first stage of what we now call France?
West Francia: Predecessor of France from 843 to 987.
The paramount leader of China since 2012, this politician served as general secretary of the Communist Party and was sent to a rural village as a teenager during the Cultural Revolution. Who is he?
Xi Jinping: Leader of China since 2012. Xi Jinping (born 15 June 1953) is a Chinese politician who is the paramount leader of China.
This Chinese politician led the Communist Party's anti-corruption watchdog from 2017 to 2022 before becoming chairman of the National People's Congress Standing Committee — who is he?
Who among these was born first?
Qian Xuesen (born 1911) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Eratosthenes (born 276 BC) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below was established earliest?
Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these was founded earliest?
MUMPS (founded 1966) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below is best known as an astronomer?
Pope Sylvester II is an astronomer.
Which one below is best known as a mathematician?
Eric Weinstein is a mathematician. Eric Ross Weinstein (born October 26, 1965) is an American investor and podcast host.
What is the atomic number of Radium?
Radium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ra and atomic number 88.
What is the atomic number of Zinc?
Zinc is a chemical element; it has symbol Zn and atomic number 30.
In what year was David Baszucki born?
David Baszucki: David Brent Baszucki (buh-ZOO-ki; born January 20, 1963) is a Canadian-born American entrepreneur, engineer, and software developer.
In what year was Arthur C. Clarke born?
Arthur C. Clarke: Clarke was a science fiction writer, an avid populariser of space travel, and a futurist of distinguished ability.
In what year was Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz born?
Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz: Leibniz, along with René Descartes and Baruch Spinoza, was one of the three influential early modern rationalists.
In what year did Bertrand Russell die?
Bertrand Russell: Bertrand Arthur William Russell, 3rd Earl Russell (18 May 1872 – 2 February 1970), was an English philosopher, logician, mathematician, and public intellectual.
In what year did Johannes Kepler die?
Johannes Kepler (27 December 1571 – 15 November 1630) was a German polymath who was an astronomer, mathematician, astrologer, natural philosopher and music theorist.
In what year was Eris discovered?
Eris (minor-planet number 136199) is the most massive and second-largest known dwarf planet in the Solar System.
Metronidazole: Pfizer. Metronidazole, sold under the brand name Flagyl and Metrogyl among others, is an antibiotic and antiprotozoal medication.
Gurjar: India. The Gurjar are an agricultural ethnic community, residing mainly in India, Pakistan, and Afghanistan, divided internally into various clan groups.
Who is credited with discovering Zirconium?
Zirconium: Martin Heinrich Klaproth. Zirconium is a chemical element; it has symbol Zr and atomic number 40.
Who is credited with discovering Quetzalcoatlus?
Quetzalcoatlus: Douglas A. Lawson. Quetzalcoatlus is a genus of azhdarchid pterosaur that lived during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous in North America.
Who is credited with discovering Silicon carbide?
Silicon carbide: Edward Goodrich Acheson. Silicon carbide (SiC), also known as carborundum, is a hard chemical compound of silicon and carbon.
Who is credited with discovering Bromine?
Bromine: Carl Jacob Löwig. Bromine is a chemical element; it has symbol Br and atomic number 35.
An economist who once worked for the IMF and later served as Prime Minister of Côte d'Ivoire from 1990 to 1993, this politician has been the country's president since 2010 — name this leader?
Alassane Ouattara (French; born 1 January 1942) is an Ivorian politician and economist who has been President of Ivory Coast (Cte d'Ivoire) since 2010.
Struck off the medical register for the fraudulent 1998 Lancet paper that falsely tied the MMR vaccine to autism, this former surgeon sparked a plunge in vaccination rates — who is he?
Andrew Wakefield (born 3 September 1956) is an English fraudster, anti-vaccine activist, and former senior surgeon.
This amino acid carries a guanidino group that serves as the body's precursor for making nitric oxide, and it's encoded by a generous six codons. Which one is it?
Arginine is the amino acid with the formula (H2N)(HN)CN(H)(CH2)3CH(NH2)CO2H.

Originating in Central Africa and classified as a hound by the American Kennel Club, this dog breed doesn't bark but instead makes an unusual yodel-like sound due to its uniquely shaped larynx — what's the breed?
Basenji is a breed of hunting dog created from stock that originated in Central Africa, including in the Republic of the Congo and other adjacent tropical African countries.
Caused by a recessive allele in the leopard but a dominant one in the jaguar, this dark melanistic variant still secretly carries its usual rosettes — what is it called?
Black panther is the melanistic colour variant of the leopard (Panthera pardus) and the jaguar (Panthera onca).

This shield-shaped insect, native to East Asia, was accidentally introduced to Allentown, Pennsylvania in 1998 and became a major agricultural pest feeding on over 100 plant species — what insect is it?
Brown marmorated stink bug (Halyomorpha halys) is an insect in the family Pentatomidae, native to China, Japan, Korea, and other Asian regions.

Made of one oxygen atom triple-bonded to a single atom of the element that also forms diamonds and graphite, this colorless, odorless, poisonous gas is slightly less dense than air and typically arises from incomplete combustion — name the compound?
Carbon monoxide (chemical formula CO) is a poisonous, flammable gas that is colorless, odorless, tasteless, and slightly less dense than air.

Native to North America except for one species found mostly in Asia, these small striped rodents are technically classified as squirrels and pack food into cheek pouches for winter storage — what are they?
Chipmunk are small, striped squirrels of subtribe Tamiina.

Making up 25 to 35 percent of protein content in mammals, this triple-helix structural protein is the main component of the extracellular matrix in cartilage, bone, tendons, and skin — name the protein?
Collagen is the main structural protein in the extracellular matrix of the connective tissues of many animals.

The first anatomically modern humans known to inhabit Europe and Siberia, arriving as early as 56,800 years ago, this population interbred with the indigenous Neanderthals before the latter went extinct — who are they?
Cro-Magnon (EEMH) were the first early modern humans (Homo sapiens) found in Europe and Siberia, continuously occupying the continent possibly from as early as 56,800 years ago.
This biological process breaks down large insoluble food compounds into small water-soluble components for absorption into the bloodstream, via both mechanical and chemical means. What is it?
Digestion is the breakdown of large insoluble food compounds into small water-soluble components so that they can be absorbed into the blood plasma.

This American theoretical physicist, a professor emeritus at Princeton's Institute for Advanced Study, is renowned for foundational contributions to string theory and topological quantum field theory — who is he?
Edward Witten (born August 26, 1951) is an American theoretical physicist known for his contributions to string theory, topological quantum field theory, and various areas of mathematics.
This class of chemical compounds forms when the hydrogen of an acid's hydroxyl group is replaced by a carbon-based group, and includes the fatty-acid derivatives called glycerides. What is it?
Ester is a compound derived from an acid (either organic or inorganic) in which the hydrogen atom (H) of at least one acidic hydroxyl group (OH) of that acid is replaced by an organyl group (R).

Species in the stinging genus Solenopsis are sometimes confused with unrelated weaver insects in Southeast Asia that share their reddish color and painful bite — what's the common name for this group?
Fire ant are several species of ants in the genus Solenopsis, which includes over 200 species.
Caused by abnormalities in the genome, this category of health problem may arise from a single faulty gene, many genes, or a chromosome abnormality — what is the general term?
Genetic disorder is a health problem caused by one or more abnormalities in the genome.
What common name covers a diverse family of marine ray-finned fish in the order Perciformes, most belonging to the genera Epinephelus or Mycteroperca?
Grouper are a diverse group of marine ray-finned fish in the family Epinephelidae, in the order Perciformes.
A member of the human Herpesviridae family, this contagious pathogen comes in two types, with about 67% of people under 50 carrying the first as of 2016. What is it?
Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1 and HSV-2) are two members of the human Herpesviridae family, a set of viruses that produce viral infections in the majority of humans.
Defined by Whipple's triad, this condition occurs when blood sugar falls below about 70 mg/dL, causing symptoms like headache, shakiness, confusion, and a fast heart rate — what's it called?

Hypoglycemia (American English), also spelled hypoglycaemia or hypoglycmia (British English), sometimes called low blood sugar, is a fall in blood sugar to levels below normal, typically below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L).
Widely planted outside its native South America for its striking purple flowers, this tree is considered Vulnerable in the wild according to the IUCN — which species?
Jacaranda mimosifolia is a sub-tropical tree native to south-central South America that has been widely planted elsewhere because of its attractive and long-lasting violet-colored flowers.
Holding doctorates in both anthropology and medicine, this SS physician earned the grim nickname 'Angel of Death' for his experiments and selections at Auschwitz — who was he?

Josef Mengele (16 March 1911 - 7 February 1979), often dubbed the "Angel of Death", was a German military officer and physician during World War II at the Soviet front and then at Auschwitz during the Holocaust.

Born of Peranakan Chinese cuisine and beloved in Singapore and Malaysia, this spicy noodle dish swims in a rich coconut-curry soup soured with tamarind, topped with prawns or chicken — what's its name?
Laksa is a spicy noodle dish popular in Southeast Asia.

The second woman to earn a physics doctorate from the University of Vienna, this Austrian-Swedish scientist became the first female full physics professor in Germany — and was instrumental in discovering nuclear fission. Who is she?
Lise Meitner (7 November 1878 - 27 October 1968) was an Austrian and Swedish nuclear physicist who was instrumental in the discovery of nuclear fission.

Made by every living organism and responsible for much of the sour taste in fruit, this dicarboxylic food additive's salt form also serves as a key intermediate in the cell's central metabolic energy cycle — what compound is it?
Malic acid is an organic compound with the molecular formula HO2CCH(OH)CH2CO2H.
This genus of about 20 species in the Lamiaceae family readily hybridizes where different species' ranges overlap, and thrives best in wet, moist soils — what genus is it?
Mentha (from Greek mntha, Linear B mi-ta), is a genus of flowering plants in the mint family, Lamiaceae.
This Nissin Food Products founder invented instant chicken ramen and went on to create the Top Ramen and Cup Noodles brands — who is he?

Momofuku Ando (March 5, 1910 - January 5, 2007), born Go Pek-Hok (Peh-e-j: G Pek-hok; Ti-l: Go Pik-hok), was a Taiwanese-born, ethnic Chinese, Japanese inventor and businessman who founded Nissin Food Products Co., Ltd.

Nicknamed for its terrifying rate of tissue destruction, this fast-spreading bacterial infection doesn't actually consume flesh — the bacteria instead release toxins that destroy it — what is this disease called?
Necrotizing fasciitis (NF), also known as flesh-eating disease or flesh-eating bacteria, is an infection that kills the body's soft tissue.

Synthesized in 2002 at a lab near Moscow and named in 2016 for the physicist who hunted down the heaviest atoms, this synthetic element claims the highest atomic number and atomic mass of anything yet known — which is it?
Oganesson is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Og and atomic number 118.
Usually numbering four and tucked behind the thyroid, these small endocrine structures release a hormone that kicks in when blood calcium runs low — which structures?
Parathyroid gland are small endocrine glands in the neck of humans and other tetrapods.
This inflammation of the back of the throat causes a sore throat and fever, most often from a viral infection, though strep bacteria cause roughly a quarter of cases in children — name the condition?
Pharyngitis is inflammation of the back of the throat, known as the pharynx.
This radioactive, silvery-gray actinide metal with atomic number 94 forms oxides in moist air that can expand a sample by up to 70% in volume — which element?
Plutonium is a chemical element; it has symbol Pu and atomic number 94.
Discovered in 1915 and too faint to see with the naked eye, which small, dim star, orbiting its two brighter neighbors once every 550,000 years, is our closest stellar neighbor after the Sun?
Proxima Centauri is the nearest star to Earth after the Sun, located 4.25 light-years (1.3 parsecs) away in the southern constellation of Centaurus.
A canine native to the southeastern United States, intermediate in size between the coyote and gray wolf. For a century its taxonomic classification has been contentious. What is it?
Red wolf (Canis rufus) is a canine native to the southeastern United States.
She co-founded a toy giant with her husband Elliot and served as its first president, but the couple resigned in 1975 amid an SEC investigation — which inventor?
Ruth Handler (ne Mosko; November 4, 1916 - April 27, 2002) was an American business magnate and inventor.
This taxonomic order groups cephalopods distinguished by having ten arms instead of eight — what order is it?
Sepiida is an order of ten-armed cephalopods.
This plant family includes both deadly poisonous species and kitchen staples like tomatoes, potatoes, and peppers, all linked by unusually high alkaloid content — what family is it?
Solanaceae is a family of flowering plants in the order Solanales.

Harvested from the seeds of the nux-vomica tree, this bitter colorless alkaloid is infamous as a poison for rodents and birds — yet was once doled out in tiny doses to stimulate the heart and bowels. What is it?
Strychnine (-nin, US chiefly -nyne) is a highly toxic, colorless, bitter, crystalline alkaloid used as a pesticide, particularly for killing small vertebrates such as birds and rodents.
Sporting beaded antennae and a pale, soft-bodied worker caste, these decaying-wood eaters belong to the order Isoptera and are really highly derived cockroaches — what are they?
Termite are a group of eusocial insects which consume a variety of decaying plant material, generally in the form of wood, leaf litter, and soil humus.
These brightly colored Neotropical birds are known for their oversized, vividly patterned bills, and their chicks hatch completely naked with no down feathers at all — what bird is it?
Toucan are Neotropical birds in the family Ramphastidae.
Measuring under five feet long, this critically endangered porpoise is endemic to a small corner of Mexico's Baja California coast — which species?
Vaquita (v-; Phocoena sinus) is a species of porpoise endemic to the northern end of the Gulf of California in Baja California, Mexico.
The largest land-dwelling member of the weasel family, this solitary, muscular carnivore of the northern boreal forests can kill prey far larger than itself — what animal is it?
Wolverine (US also; Gulo gulo), also called the carcajou or quickhatch (from East Cree, kwiihkwahaacheew), is the largest land-dwelling member of the family Mustelidae.

Introduced to the British Isles by 1500 and known there simply as 'sycamore,' this wind-tolerant maple from Central Europe can grow to 35 metres and has turned invasive in North America and Australia — which species?
Acer pseudoplatanus: Species of maple tree. It is a large deciduous, broad-leaved tree, tolerant of wind and coastal exposure.
Launched to challenge the Boeing 747, this is the world's largest passenger airliner and the only full-length double-deck jet — which aircraft, unveiled in Toulouse in 2005?
This American economist shared the 2012 Nobel for the theory of stable allocations and "market design" — applying economic theory to real-world matching problems; who is he?
Named for a 19th-century Swedish physicist and symbolized by a letter of the Swedish alphabet, which unit of length equals one ten-billionth of a metre, handy for measuring atoms and bond lengths?
Angstrom: Unit of length. The unit is named after the Swedish physicist Anders Jonas Ångström (1814–1874).

Studying humanity's past through the recovery of artifacts and sites — including stone tools dating back 3.3 million years — this discipline sits at the crossroads of the social sciences and humanities — which field?
Archaeology: Study of human activity based on materials left behind.
The third-largest fish in its family, behind Siberian taimen and Pacific Chinook, this species is unusual for surviving spawning and returning to sea to breed again — which fish?
Atlantic salmon: Species of fish. The Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) is a species of ray-finned fish in the family Salmonidae.
Also called the lammergeier, this bird of prey is the only known vertebrate whose diet is 70 to 90 percent bone — which bird?
Bearded vulture: Species of bird. The bearded vulture (Gypaetus barbatus), also known as the lammergeier and ossifrage, is a very large bird of prey in the monotypic genus Gypaetus.
Made by combining phenol and acetone, this compound forms 65 to 70 percent of the world's polycarbonate plastics production — which chemical?
Bisphenol A: Chemical used in plastics, xenoestrogen.
Hailing from the Anglo-Scottish frontier and frequently cited as the most intelligent dog breed on Earth, which sheepdog dominates sheepdog trials?
Border Collie: Working dog breed. The Border Collie is a breed of British herding dog of the collie type of medium size.
This condition involves inflamed, fluid-filled sacs that normally cushion friction near joints like the shoulder, elbow, hip and knee — what is it?
Bursitis: Inflammation of the bursae (sacs of synovial fluid in joints)
Native to the Americas, this plant genus in the nightshade family produces the fruits we call peppers, including sweet bell types and fiery chilies — what genus is it?
This bacterial skin infection affects the dermis and subcutaneous fat, most often striking the legs or face and causing spreading redness and swelling — what is it?
Cellulitis: Bacterial infection of the inner layers of the skin called the dermis.

A yellowish-green gas that turns reddish-brown liquid when cooled and bright orange crystals when colder still, this compound is usually handled in solution and used as a bleach and disinfectant — what is it?
This French inventor born near Toulouse is remembered chiefly as an aviation pioneer, but in 1870 he was also among the first to take up the sport of cycling in France — who is it?
Clément Ader: French inventor and engineer (1841–1925)
Better known as "pink eye," this inflammation of the clear layer over the white of the eye can leave a lid stuck shut by morning — what's the medical name?

Conjunctivitis: Inflammation of the eye. Conjunctivitis, also known as pink eye, is inflammation of the conjunctiva, the thin and clear layer that covers the white surface of the eye and the inner eyelid.
Commonly called comb jellies, these are the largest animals that swim using rows of cilia, drifting through every ocean as masses of two-layered jelly — what's the phylum?
Ctenophora: Phylum of gelatinous marine animals.
From muntjac to moose, members of the family Cervidae shed and regrow bony skull extensions each year — antlers used to battle rivals. What hoofed ruminant is this?
Deer: Family of hoofed mammals. A deer (pl.: deer) or true deer is a hoofed ruminant ungulate of the family Cervidae (informally the deer family).
Bred around 1890 by a Thuringian tax collector looking for a loyal guard dog, this sleek, high-alert German breed traditionally had its ears cropped and tail docked — which breed?
Dobermann: Black and tan dog breed from Germany.
Having studied mathematics under Karl Weierstrass, which philosopher founded the school of phenomenology and argued that transcendental consciousness sets the limits of all possible knowledge?
Caused by mutations in any of sixteen genes that weaken the skin's structural attachment layers, this rare inherited condition causes painful blistering from the slightest friction — which disease?
Epidermolysis bullosa: Rare medical conditions that result in easy blistering of the skin and mucous membranes.
This small woodland bird has blue-gray upperparts, a black eye-stripe, and famously plasters the entrance to its tree-hole nest with mud if it's too large — what is it?
Eurasian nuthatch: Small passerine bird species.

Named for the physicist who reportedly asked 'but where is everybody?' at Los Alamos in 1950, this puzzle questions why we've found no evidence of alien civilizations despite the odds favoring them — what's it called?
Fermi paradox: Discrepancy of the lack of evidence for alien life despite its apparent likelihood.
Called the "father of modern parasitology," this Italian physician-poet famously dismantled spontaneous generation by showing that maggots hatch from fly eggs — who was he?
Francesco Redi: Italian naturalist and poet. Francesco Redi (18 February 1626 – 1 March 1697) was an Italian physician, naturalist, biologist, and poet.
This is the largest lizard family, boasting over 950 species that cling to surfaces via Van der Waals forces in their toe hairs — including house, tokay, and day varieties — which family?
Gekkonidae: Family of lizards. Gekkonidae (the common geckos) is the largest family of geckos, containing over 950 described species in 62 genera.
Brought to market by Monsanto in 1974 under the brand name Roundup, this herbicide works by blocking a key enzyme that plants need to grow — what is it?
Glyphosate: Systemic herbicide and crop desiccant.
A founder of psychophysics, this German scientist captured how sensation relates to stimulus in a logarithmic law that now bears his and Weber's names — who was he?
Gustav Fechner: German experimental psychologist, physicist, and philosopher (1801–1887)
In their normal state these vascular cushions in the anal canal actually help with stool control; only when swollen or inflamed do they become the condition also known as piles — what is it?
Hemorrhoid: Vascular structures in the anal canal. The signs and symptoms of hemorrhoids depend on the type present.
Damage to the sympathetic trunk nerves produces this trio of symptoms on one side of the face — a constricted pupil, a droopy eyelid, and reduced sweating — what is this condition called?
Horner's syndrome: Facial disorder due to damage of the sympathetic nerves.
Marked in its severe stage by hallucinations and paradoxical undressing, which condition is defined as a body core temperature below 35 degrees Celsius?
Hypothermia: Human body core temperature below 35 °C (95 °F)
Known historically as green vitriol or copperas, this blue-green heptahydrate salt is used to treat anemia and forms a paramagnetic octahedral complex in water — which compound?
Iron(II) sulfate: Chemical compound. Iron(II) sulfate or ferrous sulfate (British English: sulphate instead of sulfate) denotes a range of salts with the formula FeSO4·xH2O.
Son of Taiwanese immigrants, this engineer launched the world's most valuable company from a Denny's restaurant in 1993 after earning a Stanford master's degree — who is he?
Jensen Huang: Taiwanese and American businessman (born 1963)
Sometimes grown just for looks, this cabbage relative's leaves can be bumpy, curly, or flat, in colors from purple to green — what leafy vegetable is it?
Kale: Form of cabbage with green or purple leaves.
Once a water retriever in Italy's Po Delta marshlands, this Italian dog breed later became prized for sniffing out truffles — which breed?
Lagotto Romagnolo: Italian breed of dog.
Cell signaling, homeostasis, metabolism, growth and reproduction are its hallmarks — and every instance of it eventually reaches death. What capacity in matter is this?
This French chemist's discoveries in fermentation and vaccination gave us a heat-treatment process that now bears his name and rabies and anthrax vaccines — who was he?
Louis Pasteur: French chemist, pharmacist and microbiologist (1822–1895)
In larger organizations it stacks into a pyramid, with a board and CEO at the top setting strategy — the broad practice of administering a business or government. What is it?
Management: Coordinating the efforts of persons.
Home to the heart, esophagus, trachea, thymus, and central chest lymph nodes, this compartment of the thoracic cavity sits between the lungs — what's it called?
Mediastinum: Central part of the thoracic cavity. The mediastinum (from Medieval Latin: mediastinus, lit. 'midway';pl.: mediastina) is the central compartment of the thoracic cavity.
This development economist shared the 2019 Nobel with Esther Duflo and Abhijit Banerjee for an experimental approach to fighting global poverty — who is he?
Michael Kremer: American economist and Nobel laureate (born 1964)
Born in Taiwan but naturalized in Japan, this businessman invented the world's first prepackaged instant noodle brand and later created Cup Noodles — who is he?
Momofuku Ando: Taiwanese-Japanese inventor and businessman (1910–2007)

It strikes when blood flow to the heart muscle stops, killing tissue — classically a crushing chest pain that radiates to the left arm or jaw, though women more often feel only neck pain or fatigue. What is this medical emergency?
Myocardial infarction: Interruption of cardiac blood supply.
A vitamer of vitamin B3 that the body can build from tryptophan, in large prescription doses it lowers LDL and raises "good" HDL cholesterol — what's this compound also called niacin?
Nicotinic acid: Organic compound and a form of vitamin B3.

With atomic number 118, this synthetic element boasts the highest atomic number and mass of any known element, and was named to honor the physicist who led the hunt for the periodic table's heaviest members — what is it?
Oganesson: Chemical element with atomic number 118 (Og)

Powered by NADH and FADH₂ handed off from glycolysis and the citric acid cycle, this mitochondrial pathway is how nearly all aerobic organisms produce ATP — far more efficiently than fermentation. What's it called?
Oxidative phosphorylation: Metabolic pathway. Oxidative phosphorylation uses these molecules and O2 to produce ATP, which is used throughout the cell whenever energy is needed.
Nicknamed the empress tree for its fast growth and showy foxglove-like blooms, which East Asian hardwood has become an invasive species across the Eastern US?
Paulownia tomentosa: Species of deciduous tree classified in its own family.
Turning colorless in acid and a fuchsia pink in base, this phthalein dye is a favorite indicator for acid-base titrations — what is it?
Phenolphthalein: pH indicator that turns pink in basic solution.
Widely planted along London's streets as a hybrid variety, this tree genus includes the sycamores of North America and can tower up to 50 meters — which genus?
Platanus: Genus of flowering plants constituting the family Platanaceae.
What is this — “Medical condition where an erection lasts excessively long”?
Priapism: Medical condition where an erection lasts excessively long. Priapism is a condition in which a penis remains erect for hours in the absence of stimulation or after stimulation has ended.
Usually caused by E. coli spreading up the urinary tract, this kidney infection typically brings fever and flank tenderness, and can be prevented by urinating after sex — what condition is it?
Pyelonephritis: Inflammation of the kidney. It is typically due to a bacterial infection, most commonly Escherichia coli.

Named after a 19th-century British naturalist employed by the East India Company, this small deer species native to south-eastern China and Taiwan has also become an established wild population in the UK and Ireland — what is it?
Reeves's muntjac: Species of deer. It has also been introduced in the United Kingdom, Ireland, the Netherlands, Belgium, and Japan.
